Keywords: retriever, vectorstore, embedding model, similarity search
Guidance: Picking a vector store or retriever type without matching it to actual data scale and query pattern (exact vs approximate, metadata filtering needs) causes either poor recall or unnecessary infrastructure overhead.
Do: Match vectorstore choice to data scale and filtering needs (e.g. pgvector for existing Postgres infra, a dedicated ANN store for very large corpora), and evaluate retrieval quality, not just latency.
Don't: Pick a vector store based on popularity alone without evaluating retrieval quality against representative queries.

Keywords: lcel, langchain expression language, chain composition, pipe operator
Guidance: Building complex logic as deeply nested Python function calls instead of LCEL's pipe composition loses built-in streaming, batching, and async support that LCEL chains get for free.
Do: Compose chains with LCEL (the | operator) to get streaming/batch/async support automatically instead of hand-rolling orchestration.
Don't: Hand-roll sequential function calls for chain logic that LCEL composition would handle with built-in streaming and async support.

Keywords: conversation memory, buffer memory, summary memory, token limit
Guidance: Using unbounded ConversationBufferMemory in a long-running chat session eventually exceeds the model's context window, causing errors or expensive truncation mid-conversation.
Do: Choose a memory strategy (buffer window, summary, or vector-store-backed) that matches expected conversation length, not an unbounded buffer by default.
Don't: Use ConversationBufferMemory with no windowing or summarization for a chat application expected to run long sessions.

Keywords: langgraph, state graph, node design, graph state schema
Guidance: A poorly-typed or overly-broad shared state object in LangGraph makes it hard to reason about what each node actually reads/writes, causing subtle bugs as the graph grows.
Do: Define a precise, typed state schema for LangGraph and have each node touch only the state keys it actually needs.
Don't: Pass a loosely-typed dict as LangGraph state that every node can read and write arbitrary keys on.
Example: class State(TypedDict):\n    messages: list\n    retrieved_docs: list

Keywords: prompt template, prompt versioning, prompt drift
Guidance: Editing prompt templates directly in application code with no version tracking makes it impossible to correlate a quality regression with a specific prompt change, or roll back cleanly.
Do: Version prompt templates (e.g. via LangSmith Hub, or plain git-tracked files) so changes are reviewable and revertible independent of code deploys.
Don't: Edit prompts inline in application code with no version history separate from the surrounding code changes.

Guidance: Debugging a multi-step chain or agent failure by reading application logs alone loses the actual intermediate prompts, tool calls, and model outputs at each step needed to find root cause.
Do: Enable LangSmith (or equivalent) tracing in non-trivial chains/agents so each step's inputs/outputs are inspectable after the fact.
Don't: Debug chain/agent failures with only high-level application logs and no step-by-step trace of prompts and outputs.

Topic: Token cost from chained LLM calls
Keywords: token cost, chained calls, cost explosion, chain depth
Guidance: Each additional step in a multi-call chain (retrieval, rewriting, grading, generation) multiplies token cost and latency; unexamined chain depth can make a simple query cost far more than it should.
Do: Measure per-request token cost/latency across the full chain and cut steps that don't measurably improve output quality.
Don't: Add chain steps (query rewriting, self-critique, re-ranking) without measuring whether each one earns its added cost and latency.
Example: # track cumulative tokens across all chain/agent steps per request, not just the final call

Keywords: streaming, astream, time to first token, perceived latency
Guidance: Waiting for a full chain/agent response before showing anything to the user makes multi-second LLM latency feel far worse than it needs to; streaming shows progress immediately.
Do: Use .stream()/.astream() (or LangGraph's streaming modes) to surface tokens/intermediate steps to the user as they're generated.
Don't: Block on the full chain response before displaying anything to the user for a multi-second generation.
Example: for chunk in chain.stream(input):\n    print(chunk, end='')

Keywords: text splitter, chunk size, chunk overlap, rag chunking
Guidance: A chunk size that's too large dilutes retrieval relevance with irrelevant surrounding text, while too small loses necessary context -- the default RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter settings rarely fit every corpus.
Do: Tune chunk size/overlap to the actual document structure (e.g. respect section boundaries) and evaluate retrieval quality with representative queries, not default splitter settings alone.
Don't: Use default text splitter chunk size/overlap for every document type without evaluating retrieval quality.

Keywords: output parser, structured output, json mode, parsing failure
Guidance: Parsing free-form LLM text output with regex/string matching breaks unpredictably when the model phrases things slightly differently than expected.
Do: Use structured output (tool calling / JSON mode / Pydantic output parsers) instead of regex-parsing free-form text for anything downstream code depends on.
Don't: Parse free-form model text output with regex for data that downstream code needs reliably structured.

Keywords: react agent, tool calling, agent executor, langgraph agent
Guidance: Using the older deprecated AgentExecutor abstraction instead of LangGraph's prebuilt/custom agent patterns loses fine-grained control over state, interrupts, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints.
Do: Build new tool-calling agents on LangGraph (create_react_agent or a custom graph) rather than the legacy AgentExecutor.
Don't: Start a new agent project on the deprecated AgentExecutor abstraction in 2026.

Keywords: llm cache, response caching, repeated prompt, cache backend
Guidance: Re-sending an identical prompt to the LLM on every request (common in dev/test loops or repeated evaluation runs) pays full token cost and latency for a response that hasn't changed.
Do: Enable a cache backend (in-memory for dev, Redis/SQLite for shared use) for deterministic, repeated prompts.
Don't: Hit the LLM API fresh for identical prompts repeated during development, testing, or evaluation runs.
